beats.narration: Begin by framing Computational Thinking Foundations as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Consider this worked case: A problem statement defines what the program must do, while input and output examples specify the expected behavior for specific cases. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.

beats.narration: Now define Variables and State precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Consider this worked case: A variable stores a value that can change over time, while expressions compute new values based on existing ones, and control structures determine which operations to execute. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Variables and State
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a table with columns for variable name, initial value, and final value, illustrating how state changes during execution.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Functions and Decomposition operates in a concrete sequence. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Consider this worked case: A function takes input parameters, performs a specific operation, and returns a result, breaking down complex problems into manageable parts. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Functions and Decomposition
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a diagram of a function with input parameters, internal operations, and a return value, showing how it encapsulates a specific task.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Recursion and Base Cases and make the decision criteria explicit. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Consider this worked case: A recursive function calls itself with a smaller input until it reaches a base case, at which point it stops and returns a value. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Recursion and Base Cases
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a tree diagram representing the recursive calls, with the base case at the bottom and each level representing a smaller instance of the problem.

beats.narration: Apply Lists and Data Structures to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Consider this worked case: A list stores items in order, a stack adds and removes items from the top, a queue adds items to the back and removes from the front, a tree organizes items hierarchically, and a graph connects entities with edges. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Lists and Data Structures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a series of diagrams showing a list, stack, queue, tree, and graph, with labels indicating the order of elements and connections.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Control Structures, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Consider this worked case: An if statement executes a block of code if a condition is true, while a for loop repeats a block of code a specified number of times. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Control Structures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart with an if statement branching into two paths and a for loop with a counter variable, illustrating how control structures direct execution.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Search and Sort Algorithms with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Consider this worked case: A search algorithm finds a specific item in a list, while a sort algorithm arranges items in order, both relying on the data structure used and specific invariants to maintain correctness. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Search and Sort Algorithms
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a table with columns for algorithm name, input, output, and invariant, showing how different algorithms handle data and maintain specific properties.

beats.narration: Use Correctness and Testing to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases. Consider this worked case: Tests verify that the program behaves as expected for various inputs, including edge cases, while tracing follows the execution step by step to identify errors. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Correctness and Testing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a table with columns for test case, expected output, actual output, and status, illustrating how tests compare intended and observable behavior.

beats.narration: Connect Debugging Techniques to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns. Consider this worked case: Debugging involves identifying and fixing errors in the code, such as syntax errors, runtime errors, or logical errors, by breaking the problem into smaller parts and focusing on one concern at a time. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Debugging Techniques
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a flowchart showing the process of debugging, with steps for identifying the error, isolating the issue, and applying a fix, with arrows indicating the flow of the process.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Assignments (both in class and for homework) requiring a pseudo code solution and an implementation are an integral part of the course. Consider this worked case: The project involves writing pseudo code to describe the algorithm, then implementing the algorithm in a programming language, and finally testing the implementation to ensure correctness. Trace each intermediate state in the example, connect it to the formal claim, and verify that the final result satisfies the stated condition. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a checklist with items for pseudo code, implementation, testing, and documentation, with checkboxes indicating completion of each step.

sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.excerpt: This course serves as an introduction to computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Specific topics covered include: expression of algorithms in pseudo code and a programming language; functional and imperative programming techniques; control structures; problem solving using recursion; basic searching and sorting; elementary data structures such as lists, trees, and graphs; and correctness, testing and debugging. Assignments (both in class and for homework) requiring a pseudo code solution and an implementation are an integral part of the course. An end-of-term project is also required. Contact Hours: Lecture/Lab 6 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective, GE: Mathematical Perspective, NTID Math Processes, SMTL: Science/Math Literacy Typically Offered: F

sources.excerpt: The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior.
